title: A heap of size k
sub: The k-th largest in O(n log k), quickselect in O(n) on average, EnqueueDequeue and your own heap for Unity
cards/0/body:
Kth Largest Element in an Array (LeetCode #215). Given an array nums and a number k, return the k-th largest element — the k-th in descending sorted order, not the k-th distinct value: in [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6] with k = 4 the answer is 4, because the descending order is 6, 5, 5, 4. Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, |nums[i]| ≤ 10⁴, and the statement explicitly asks you to do it without sorting.

Signals that a heap will help:

1. You need not the whole order, only the k best (or worst), or the k-th of them.
2. You need the current minimum or maximum of a changing set again and again: take the best one out, put a new one in.
3. The data arrives as a stream, and the answer is needed after every element or at any moment.

Here it is signal 1. In the related problem Kth Largest Element in a Stream (#703), signal 3 joins it.
cards/1/q: Which problems does a heap solve? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: Once a second a server takes the job with the earliest deadline from a queue, and new jobs keep arriving
cards/1/options/1: The top 10 scores out of a million leaderboard records
cards/1/options/2: After each new number of a stream, report the third largest so far
cards/1/options/3: Find two numbers in an array that add up to target
cards/1/options/4: The longest substring without repeating characters
cards/1/explain: The job queue is signal 2: the minimum deadline, again and again, from a set that keeps changing. The leaderboard is signal 1: you need 10 out of a million, not the whole order. The third largest after each number is signals 1 and 3 — that is exactly #703. A pair with sum target is a partner by exact value, so a hash map. A substring without repeats is a sliding window.
cards/2/body:
Sort and take the element at index n − k. Array.Sort is O(n log n): for n = 10⁵ that is about 1.7·10⁶ comparisons, which by the rule of thumb of 10⁸ operations per second is milliseconds. Time-wise sorting passes, and you should say so out loud in the interview. It is rejected for other reasons:

1. Wasted work: all n elements get ordered, while you need one.
2. Array.Sort sorts in place and destroys the input — or you copy it, which is O(n) memory.
3. It does not work on a stream: every new element means sorting again or inserting into the middle of an array in O(n).

Find and strike out the maximum k times — O(n·k). Fine for a small k, but k can be anything up to n.
cards/3/q: n = 10⁵, k = n / 2. How many operations does “find and strike out the maximum k times” take, and what follows?
cards/3/options/0: ≈ 5·10⁹ — tens of seconds, the solution will not pass
cards/3/options/2: ≈ 10⁵ — a single pass over the array
cards/3/explain: Each maximum search is a pass over n elements, and there are k passes: n·k = 10⁵ · 5·10⁴ = 5·10⁹. At about 10⁸ operations per second that is around 50 seconds against a limit of 1–2. Sorting is thousands of times cheaper. A heap of k elements with k = n / 2 costs about as much as sorting — n log k ≈ 1.6·10⁶; it pulls ahead when k is small.
cards/3/wrong/1: 1.7·10⁶ is n log n for sorting. Here you make k full passes over the array: n·k.
cards/3/wrong/2: One pass finds one maximum. To get to the k-th you need k passes.
cards/4/title: The idea: a min-heap of k elements
cards/4/body:
The brute force searches for the maximum among everything every time, although you only need to remember the k best seen so far. Keep them in a min-heap (how it works is in the lesson on .NET collections: the minimum sits at the root, insertion and removal are O(log size)). The root is the worst of the best, the entry threshold into the top k. The priority is the number itself: Enqueue(x, x). With priority −x the same queue would become a max-heap.

Put every new x into the heap. If it now holds k + 1 elements, Dequeue removes the minimum: it is definitely not among the k largest, since there are k numbers above it.

Invariant: after i elements the heap holds exactly the min(i, k) largest of them, and the root is the k-th largest of those seen. So the answer is Peek() after the pass.

Cost: n insertions at O(log k) each — O(n log k), memory O(k). For n = 10⁶ and k = 10 that is about 3.3·10⁶ steps against 2·10⁷ for sorting. The arrival order does not matter, and you do not need the whole array at once — you can even read it from a file.

Why min and not max: what you need to know quickly is whom to throw out — the weakest of the strong. A max-heap over all n elements also gives the answer (k times Dequeue), but that is O(n) memory, and n insertions cost O(n log n).

In a game: the top 10 scores on a leaderboard, the k most dangerous threats for the AI, the k nearest targets.
cards/4/flow/4: the root is the k-th largest
cards/5/q: Assemble the solution with a min-heap of k elements.
cards/5/explain: Priority x gives a min-heap with the smallest at the root; with −x the root would be the maximum, and the best elements would be thrown out. Remove once there are k + 1 elements: the condition is Count > k. With >= the heap would keep k − 1 elements, and Peek would return the (k − 1)-th largest. At the end the root is the k-th largest: Peek(), without removing it.
cards/6/task: Step through the trace on [4, 1, 7, 3, 8, 5, 9, 2], k = 3. The rig stops twice and asks what Dequeue will do. Watch the root: it is the entry threshold into the top three.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: 9 has arrived: the heap holds 5, 8, 7, 9, size 4 > k. The code calls Dequeue. What will the root be?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: Dequeue removes the minimum 5. The last element of the array, 9, takes its place and sinks towards the smaller child: 7 < 8, so it swaps with 7. The heap is 7, 8, 9 with root 7. These are the top three seen so far, and 7 is the new threshold.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: 2 has arrived — below the threshold 7. The code still called Enqueue, and the 2 rose to the root: 2, 7, 9, 8. What will Dequeue remove?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: Dequeue removes the minimum — the 2 itself. The heap is back to 7, 8, 9: the 2 came in and went out, paying for a sift up and a sift down, O(log k) twice. Such a number can be rejected by comparing it with the threshold before inserting — how PriorityQueue does that is in the next card.
cards/7/body:
EnqueueDequeue(x, p) (.NET 6) is “add, then immediately take the minimum” in one operation. If the queue is empty or p is not greater than the root’s priority, the method returns x right away and leaves the heap alone. Otherwise x takes the root’s place and sinks — one sift instead of two — and the old root is returned. For “the k best”: the first k elements go in with Enqueue, and from then on only EnqueueDequeue.

DequeueEnqueue(x, p) (.NET 8) is the other way round: it removes the root first and then adds x, even if x is worse. In “the k best” that is a bug: the threshold is thrown out even when x should not get in.

Descending priority means a max-heap. Two ways: the comparer Comparer<int>.Create((a, b) => b.CompareTo(a)), or priority −x with the normal comparison. −x is faster (why — in “Deeper” on the card about your own heap), but it breaks on int.MinValue: in unchecked arithmetic −int.MinValue == int.MinValue, so the smallest number gets the most urgent priority. The comparer b − a instead of b.CompareTo(a) overflows the same way.

Last Stone Weight (#1046): each turn, smash the two heaviest stones y ≥ x. If y = x, both vanish; otherwise a stone of weight y − x remains. Return the weight of the last stone, or 0. “The two maximums, again and again” is signal 2: a max-heap, O(n log n). Re-sorting on every turn is O(n² log n).
cards/8/task: Step through the Last Stone Weight trace on [2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 1]. The root of the max-heap is the heaviest stone. The rig will ask about the turn with equal stones.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Smashes two stones of 1: both vanish, one stone is left — the answer is 1
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Smashes two stones of 1 and puts a stone of weight 0 back into the heap
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Stops: all stones are equal, the answer is 0
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: The heap holds three stones of weight 1. What does the code do on this turn?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: y = x = 1, so the condition y != x is false — nothing goes back into the heap. One stone is left, Count = 1, the loop ends: the answer is its weight, 1. A zero in the heap would not spoil the answer (smashing against zero changes nothing), but it is an extra turn, and the code does not make it.
cards/9/body:
The k-th largest is the element that would land at index n − k after an ascending sort. Quickselect is half of quicksort: partition the range around a pivot and continue only into the part that contains that index.

Three-way partition: smaller than the pivot on the left, equal in the middle, greater on the right. If the index you need falls into the block of equals, you are done.

Cost. With good pivots the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n — O(n) on average. In the worst case the pivot is an extreme every time and the range shrinks by one element — O(n²), which for n = 10⁵ is 5·10⁹. That is why the pivot is chosen at random: the worst case does not disappear, but it becomes vanishingly unlikely. A “first element” pivot on already sorted input gives exactly the square.

Duplicates. A plain two-way partition (the Lomuto scheme) on an array of identical numbers cuts off one element at a time — O(n²) whatever the pivot. A three-way partition gathers all the equal ones in the middle in a single pass.

The price: it rearranges the input in place (a copy is O(n) memory), and it needs the whole array at once — it does not work on a stream. Array and List<T> have no ready-made “select the k-th”; you write it by hand.
cards/10/q: A game server receives 10⁷ match results a day and once a minute shows the top 100 of the day. What do you choose?
cards/10/options/0: A min-heap of 100 elements: each result is one comparison with the root, plus O(log 100) if it gets in
cards/10/options/1: Store all results and run quickselect once a minute: it is O(n), faster than a heap
cards/10/options/2: Store all results and sort them once a minute
cards/10/explain: This is a stream (signal 3), and k is small. A heap of 100 elements is ready at any moment: the top 100 sit in it, and printing them costs 100 · log 100 operations. Memory is 100 records, not 10⁷. Quickselect and sorting need to keep everything and go over the whole backlog again every minute.
cards/10/wrong/1: O(n) is per run over everything collected. Once a minute that is up to 10⁷ operations and 10⁷ records in memory, while the heap is updated in O(log k) per result and is always ready.
cards/10/wrong/2: Sorting everything collected once a minute is O(n log n) over and over, plus memory for all 10⁷ records. And you only need 100.
cards/11/title: Unity: your own binary heap on an array
cards/11/body:
Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) has no PriorityQueue, so you write your own heap. In Unity interviews you are often asked to write one from scratch — and they expect code with no off-by-one bugs. What matters:

1. Indices. Node i has parent (i − 1) / 2 and children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. The right child may be missing — hence the check c + 1 < n.
2. A “hole” instead of swaps. When sifting up, do not swap elements at every step: move the parent down and write x once at the end. Half as many writes.
3. Clear the slot. After Pop write a[n] = default: if T is a reference type, the stale reference would otherwise keep the object alive for the collector.
4. Zero allocations. The array grows by doubling; once warmed up, Push and Pop allocate nothing.
5. PushPop mirrors EnqueueDequeue: if x is not greater than the root, return it right away.

A max-heap is the same heap with a descending comparer.
cards/11/deep:
How .NET does it. PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> keeps a single array of tuples (TElement Element, TPriority Priority)[]; the constructor without a capacity starts with an empty array, and it grows by doubling, but by at least 4 elements. The heap is 4-ary (Arity = 4): parent (i − 1) >> 2, first child (i << 2) + 1. Sifting up and down uses the same “hole” as above, and the vacated slot is cleared only if the tuple contains references (RuntimeHelpers.IsReferenceOrContainsReferences).

Why −x is faster than a comparer. If TPriority is a value type and no comparer was passed (or Comparer<T>.Default was passed), the queue stores null instead of a comparer and takes a separate path with Comparer<TPriority>.Default.Compare — the JIT devirtualizes and inlines that call. A custom IComparer is an interface call on every comparison. The difference only shows on a hot path, but you should know the answer to “why”.

A struct comparer in your own heap. The same trick works for your heap: MinHeap<T, TCmp> where TCmp : struct, IComparer<T> with a field TCmp cmp. For a value-type TCmp the JIT compiles a separate copy of the code per type, and Compare is called directly, not through the interface; IL2CPP with IL2CPP Code Generation = Faster runtime (the default) also generates separate code for value-type arguments, so the call becomes direct; in Faster (smaller) builds mode generic code is shared across all arguments, and the gain may be lost.

Building in O(n). From an existing array the heap is built bottom-up: SiftDown for i from n / 2 − 1 down to 0. There are about n / 2ʰ⁺¹ nodes at height h, and each sinks at most h levels: the total n · Σ h / 2ʰ⁺¹ ≤ n. That is how the PriorityQueue constructor from a collection and EnqueueRange into an empty queue work.

What else is missing. Remove(element, out …) only appeared in .NET 9 and costs O(n): it searches for the element linearly. There is no priority update at all — lazy deletion replaces it, covered in the lesson on merging and the median. EnsureCapacity and TrimExcess exist since .NET 6.
cards/12/q: After a series of Pop calls, a custom heap of positive numbers returned 0, although nobody ever pushed a zero. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/12/explain: The check c + 1 < n is missing: the last internal node may have only a left child. Then a[c + 1] is a[n] — the slot past the end of the heap, where Pop has just written default, that is 0. On the heap 1, 5, 3: Pop removes 1, n = 2, a[2] = 0; SiftDown sees a “child” 0 < 5, picks it and lifts 0 into the root, while 3 is pushed past the end. Hence the zero.
cards/13/q: You are solving Kth Largest Element out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/13/items/0: Clarify: k-th in sorted order or among distinct values, may the array be modified, what are n and k
cards/13/items/1: Name sorting: O(n log n), it passes, but it is wasted work and fails on a stream
cards/13/items/2: Idea: keep only the k best in a min-heap; the root is the entry threshold
cards/13/items/3: Write the code, stating the invariant: the heap holds the k largest seen so far
cards/13/items/4: Run [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2, and show when the root gets removed
cards/13/items/5: State the complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) memory
cards/13/items/6: Alternative: quickselect — O(n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case, destroys the input
cards/13/explain: First agree on the statement — “k-th among distinct values” is a different problem, and a ban on modifying the array rules out quickselect without a copy. Then the baseline, the idea with its invariant, the code, a dry run, the complexity. Quickselect comes last, as the answer to “can you do better?”, with its honest price.
